questions.learningObjective: Explain why a feed can create addiction loops
questions.stem: During a field survey, a biologist finds herself scrolling a feed for an hour without deciding to; what design feature drives this?

answer.exemplar: Infinite scroll removes natural stopping points, so the feed can keep her engaged without a conscious decision to continue.

questions.explanation: Infinite scroll eliminates stopping cues. That is the design feature behind unintended long sessions.
questions.hint: Ask what removes the natural pause.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A filter bubble and the mechanism that forms it
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a filter bubble's effect on expertise

stimulus.body: A biologist's feed shows only amateur birding tips; professional ornithology papers never appear, though she follows several researchers.

questions.stem: During a field survey, the scenario above occurs; what is the likely cause?

options.text: Papers are not allowed on feeds

questions.explanation: Engagement filtering can favour simpler, more clickable content. Supply loss, blocking and platform rules are unsupported.
questions.hint: Ask what the algorithm rewards.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A meme and how it transmits
questions.learningObjective: Identify a meme's template reuse
questions.stem: During a field survey, a biologist sees the same frog image with new text in five different contexts; what is being reused?

options.text: The template image, with new text each time

questions.explanation: The image template persists while text changes. Fixed captions, authorship and algorithm are not what is reused.
questions.hint: Ask what stays the same across versions.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A hashtag and the work it does
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a hashtag's search function
questions.stem: During a field survey, a biologist searches a hashtag and finds posts from three years ago; what does this show?

options.text: Hashtags create a persistent, searchable archive

options.misconception: treats old content as a mistake

questions.explanation: Hashtags persist as searchable archives. Recency, revival and error are not what the search shows.
questions.hint: Ask what a search across time reveals.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: An algorithm and the ranking it produces
questions.learningObjective: Summarise what an algorithm cannot know
questions.stem: During a field survey, a biologist expects a search engine to understand her research intent; why is that expectation misplaced?

answer.exemplar: The engine matches patterns in queries and behaviour; it does not grasp her scientific intent or judge truth.

questions.explanation: Algorithms match signals, not meaning. They cannot verify truth or intent.
questions.hint: Separate pattern matching from understanding.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A livestream and its interaction model
questions.learningObjective: Identify a livestream's data cost

stimulus.body: A biologist streams 4K video from a remote site for 30 minutes on a metered mobile plan.

questions.stem: During a field survey, the scenario above occurs; what is the main practical risk?
questions.explanation: 4K streaming on a metered plan risks high data cost. Illegality, viewing and sharpness are not the practical risk.
questions.hint: Ask what 4K streaming costs on mobile data.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A screen-time report and what it measures
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a report that ignores multitasking
questions.stem: During a field survey, a biologist's screen-time report counts two apps used simultaneously as separate hours; what distortion results?

options.text: Total time is inflated beyond actual elapsed time

questions.explanation: Counting simultaneous apps separately inflates total time beyond elapsed time. Accuracy, deletion and impossibility are wrong.
questions.hint: Ask how simultaneous use should be counted.

questions.explanation: Daily return is retention optimisation. Well-being, randomness and short sessions are not the goal.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A filter bubble and the mechanism that forms it
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a filter bubble is not a conspiracy
questions.stem: During a field survey, a biologist attributes her narrow feed to a deliberate plot; why is that explanation usually wrong?

answer.exemplar: Filter bubbles typically emerge from automated personalisation based on her own clicks, not from a coordinated human plot.

questions.explanation: Automated personalisation based on behaviour explains most narrowing. A plot is an overreach.
questions.hint: Ask what mechanism actually narrows the feed.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A meme and how it transmits
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a meme's speed advantage

stimulus.body: A joke image about a frog appears on four platforms within two hours of a news event, each version slightly different.

questions.stem: During a field survey, the scenario above occurs; what does it illustrate?

options.misconception: confuses meme speed with event truth

options.text: Memes spread fast through low-friction remixing

questions.explanation: Fast, slightly varied spread shows low-friction remixing. Event falsity, coordination and professional tools are wrong.
questions.hint: Ask how so many variants appeared so fast.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a hashtag from a keyword search
questions.stem: During a field survey, a biologist wonders why a hashtag search differs from a keyword search; what is the key difference?

options.text: Hashtags are user-applied labels; keywords match text anywhere

questions.explanation: Hashtags rely on user-applied labels; keyword search matches text anywhere. Accuracy, recency and no-difference are wrong.

questions.learningObjective: Recognise when ranking reflects A/B testing
questions.stem: During a field survey, a biologist notices the same search alternates between two layouts on refresh; what is most likely happening?

options.text: The platform is running an A/B test

questions.topic: A livestream and its interaction model
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a livestream builds parasocial bonds
questions.stem: During a field survey, a biologist's viewers feel they know her after weekly streams; what interaction feature drives this?

answer.exemplar: Regular, real-time presence with direct address creates a sense of personal relationship despite the one-sided broadcast.

questions.explanation: Repeated real-time presence and direct address foster parasocial bonds. The bond persists despite one-sidedness.
questions.hint: Think about repeated real-time contact.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A screen-time report and what it measures
questions.learningObjective: Assess a report that lacks context

stimulus.body: Report: 'Daily screen time: 7h 45m. No breakdown by app, no context, no comparison to prior weeks.'

questions.stem: During a field survey, a biologist reads the report above; what is its main weakness?

options.text: It gives a total without usable context

questions.explanation: A bare total without breakdown or trend cannot guide action. Too-much, fake and unmeasurable are wrong.
questions.hint: Ask what the number alone cannot show.

questions.stem: During a field survey, a biologist summarises what a recommendation feed ultimately optimises for; which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Attention and engagement that benefit the platform
